memory_leads.lead: Many ports separate a public or quasi-public port-authority/landlord role from terminal operating companies: the landlord controls scarce waterfront/land and long-horizon development while operators run cargo facilities under leases, concessions or similar rights.

Terminal concessions or long leases are a durable capacity-allocation mechanism: they can combine operating rights, investment obligations, performance expectations and return economics over periods much longer than a shipping service cycle; exact contract terms are deferred.

Common-user terminals and dedicated or preferential facilities create different access structures. Dedicated capacity can improve coordination for an anchor carrier or cargo system while changing contestability and residual capacity available to others.

Shipping-line terminal affiliates and independent terminal operators create different vertical-integration relationships between vessel networks and shore capacity; the structural issue is control/alignment of terminal capacity, not a ranking of terminal groups.

Berth capacity is jointly constrained by berth length/number, water depth and nautical access, vessel-size compatibility and occupancy pattern; adding nominal quay length does not automatically create usable calls for every ship class.
Yard and land are independent terminal capacity pools. Longer container or cargo dwell can exhaust ground slots and internal circulation even when berth and crane capacity remain available.

Gate complexes, road access and on-dock/near-dock rail or barge interfaces are infrastructure capacity rather than merely downstream operations; weak interchange capacity can make a marine terminal effectively smaller than its quay rating.

Channels, dredging, turning basins, breakwaters and other nautical-access works often sit outside the terminal operator's direct control yet condition the size, tide window and reliability of vessels the terminal can serve.

Quay cranes, yard cranes, horizontal transport systems, reefer power, gate systems and maintenance facilities are lumpy terminal capex. Equipment expansion can shift rather than eliminate the bottleneck if land, labor, berth or inland evacuation remains binding.

Terminal automation is a coupled redesign of equipment, yard layout, software/control systems, maintenance skills and labor interfaces rather than a standalone machine purchase; transition periods can carry execution risk.

Permitting, environmental review, community/land-use constraints and construction staging can make port expansion a long-lead supply response. Demand can therefore outrun infrastructure even when operators already believe more capacity is needed.

Concession economics may use rents, revenue/throughput-linked payments, minimum commitments or investment obligations to divide risk between landlord and operator; the useful memory is the incentive architecture, while exact clauses and tariffs require Evidence.

Port and terminal expansion can involve infrastructure investors, banks, public finance or strategic operators because assets are capital intensive and long lived. Financing horizon and demand uncertainty therefore influence when announced capacity becomes physically available.

Carrier consolidation and alliance/network concentration refine the atlas liner-scale theme because fewer large customers can influence terminal location, dedicated-capacity decisions and bargaining over long-horizon investments.

Congestion is not only an operating-state variable: repeated high utilization and dwell can become the signal that triggers debottlenecking, yard reconfiguration or expansion plans, while temporary shocks can also induce overbuilding if mistaken for structural demand.

The atlas capacity-lag mechanism applies to terminals as well as ships: long permitting/construction cycles can produce alternating scarcity and excess capacity when projects complete after trade patterns, vessel deployment or congestion conditions have changed.

Resilience can conflict with peak utilization: spare land, redundant gates/berths, alternative access or recovery space may look inefficient in normal periods but preserve throughput during equipment outages, surges or disrupted schedules.

Crane, gang and cargo-handling productivity as immediate effective-capacity drivers were already captured by P014; P021 retains only their relationship to long-horizon asset investment and governance.
Gate, rail/barge and inland handoff congestion were already captured operationally in P020; P021 retains only the infrastructure ownership and capacity-investment layer behind those interfaces.

reviewed_no_specific_memory.reason: Blind memory supports the structural concession/lease category but not exact duration, exclusivity, rent, throughput, investment or termination clauses for particular ports.
Exact capex, TEU/tonnage ratings, commissioning dates and project outcomes require dated Evidence.
Rules, fees and approval regimes vary by jurisdiction and period and cannot be treated as one generic historical fact.
No reliable blind basis exists for exhaustive ownership histories or rankings across public/private and regional terminal systems.

stop_reason: The port/terminal governance and capacity-creation chain is populated from landlord/authority through concession/operator structure, scarce land/nautical access, terminal and interchange capex, financing and long-lead expansion. Further recall becomes port-, project-, contract-, tariff-, regulatory- or company-specific.

method_observation.observation: For infrastructure-heavy industry memory, physical capacity should be activated together with the rights, land/access control, investment obligations and financing states that determine whether an asset can be expanded or used; otherwise a component catalog misses the durable governance bottleneck.

truth_boundary: Memory-only orientation; no port ownership, concession term, terminal capacity, project cost/date, tariff, permitting outcome, regulatory rule or company-specific investment fact is verified.
